opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. The way I see it, we've been fighting physics for decades, and physics is starting to win.

Look at how we compute today. Digital computing is built on the idea that every bit has to be pristine, a clean zero or a clean one. To keep those bits deterministic, you have to drive transistors hard enough that thermal noise basically never flips them. That means spending energy to stay well above the noise floor, and every irreversible operation you do dissipates heat on top of that. As transistors shrink toward atomic scales, the noise doesn't go away. It becomes a bigger fraction of the signal. So we keep paying more and more energy just to suppress the natural fluctuations of matter.

Meanwhile, look at what we actually use all that compute for in AI. A huge amount of it is probabilistic: sampling from distributions, diffusion models, Bayesian inference, energy-based models, Monte Carlo methods. We spend enormous energy making hardware perfectly deterministic, and then we spend more energy running pseudorandom number generators to put the randomness back in. That's absurd from a first-principles standpoint.

Thermodynamic computing flips this. Instead of treating thermal noise as the enemy, you treat it as a resource. You build physical systems whose natural dynamics, their equilibration and fluctuations, *are* the computation. If your hardware's energy landscape encodes the distribution you care about, the system samples from it for free, just by relaxing physically. You're harnessing the universe's own tendency to explore state space instead of simulating it bit by bit.

So I don't think it's a matter of if, it's when. If you want to keep scaling intelligence, and I think civilization should, you can't keep throwing gigawatts at deterministic simulations of stochastic processes. Eventually you have to match the substrate to the algorithm, and for generative AI that substrate is fundamentally thermodynamic. It's the path of least resistance, literally, for physics.

r001.rationale: The response discusses thermal noise becoming more significant as transistors shrink, but does not mention discrete electric charge or noise caused by using very little charge.

r002.rationale: It argues that suppressing noise becomes costly as hardware scales and advocates thermodynamic computing, but does not identify noise at very low charge as the reason for that transition.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the way I think about it is that computing is ultimately a physical process. Every bit flip is a physical event, and physics sets the rules for how cheaply you can do it. Right now we build digital computers out of transistors, and we spend enormous amounts of energy fighting against noise. We take a transistor, which is fundamentally a noisy analog device, and we pump enough voltage through it that the thermal fluctuations become negligible, so we can pretend it's a clean, deterministic switch. That's where most of the energy goes. We're paying a thermodynamic tax to suppress randomness.

And the thing is, we've been riding Moore's law and Dennard scaling for decades, but Dennard scaling broke down a while ago. We can't keep dropping the voltage, because as you shrink transistors and lower voltage, you get closer to the thermal noise floor, kT, and the devices start making errors. So we're hitting a wall where the energy per operation is only a few orders of magnitude above the Landauer limit, and the remaining gap is basically the cost of enforcing determinism on a stochastic substrate.

So you have to ask, what are we actually computing? And if you look at where compute demand is exploding, it's AI. It's neural networks, it's probabilistic inference, it's sampling, it's Monte Carlo, it's generative models that are literally learning distributions and then sampling from them. These are algorithms that want randomness. We spend energy to kill the noise in the hardware, and then we spend more energy running pseudorandom number generators and sampling routines in software to put the noise back in. That's absurd from a physics standpoint.

Thermodynamic computing is the idea that you stop fighting the physics and start using it. You build physical systems whose natural dynamics, as they relax toward thermal equilibrium, implement the computation you care about. The fluctuations become a resource instead of a bug. A system sitting in a heat bath at temperature T is already sampling from a Boltzmann distribution for free. Nature does that without any clock cycles. So if you can encode your problem, say the energy landscape of your model, into the physical energy landscape of the device, then the hardware just settles into the answer, and the entropy from the environment is doing the work for you.

In the long run I think this is unavoidable, because the only way to keep driving energy per operation down is to get closer to the fundamental thermodynamic limits, and you can't do that while insisting on deterministic digital abstraction everywhere. You have to let the computation be as noisy as the physics is, and design algorithms that are natively compatible with that. In a sense, it's the same reason biology is so efficient. The brain runs on about twenty watts, and it's a warm, wet, noisy system operating right near the thermal regime. It never tried to be a digital computer. I think the future of efficient compute looks a lot more like that than like a ever-cleaner version of what we have now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses thermal noise in transistors as voltage and device size decrease, but does not explain that discreteness of electric charge makes noise unavoidable at very low charge.

r002.rationale: It connects thermal noise and errors near the noise floor to the eventual need for thermodynamic computing, but does not identify noise at very low charge as the reason.

astra-6.text:
Well, fundamentally, computation is a physical process. We tend to abstract that away and think about bits and logic gates, but underneath, you’re moving charge around and dissipating energy. And as you push the energy per operation down, thermal fluctuations become increasingly important. You can’t keep treating them as a negligible perturbation forever.

In conventional computing, we spend energy making the dynamics very reliable: a bit is definitely zero or definitely one, and noise is something to suppress. But a lot of the computations we want to do in machine learning are inherently probabilistic. We want to sample from distributions, explore possibilities, and find configurations that satisfy constraints. So there’s an opportunity to use those thermal fluctuations as part of the computation rather than spending energy fighting them and then generating randomness separately.

The idea is to engineer a physical system whose dynamics perform the computation you care about. You encode the problem into its interactions, let it evolve, and read out the result. Of course, preparing the system, controlling it, and reading it out all have costs—you have to count those too.

So I wouldn’t say every computer has to become a thermal sampler. But if we want to keep reducing energy consumption, eventually we have to design algorithms and hardware together with the thermodynamics in mind. The physics stops being something hidden beneath the abstraction and becomes a computational resource.

r001.rationale: The response says thermal fluctuations become important as energy per operation falls, but it does not connect unavoidable noise to the discreteness of electric charge or to using very little charge.

r002.rationale: The response argues that lower energy use makes thermodynamics relevant, but it does not identify noise at very low charge as the reason computing must become thermodynamic.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the key distinction is between the energy you need to perform a computation and the energy we happen to spend implementing it today. In conventional digital computing, we spend a lot of energy making every operation behave deterministically, keeping signals clean and moving information around. But as you reduce the energy associated with those signals, thermal fluctuations become increasingly important. You can’t just keep turning the voltage down and expect the same abstraction to hold indefinitely.

So eventually you have to ask: can we make those fluctuations part of the computation rather than spending energy suppressing them? That’s the idea behind thermodynamic computing. You engineer a physical system whose dynamics do useful computational work—for example, relaxing toward a distribution you want to sample from.

There’s also a fundamental distinction between logically reversible operations and erasing information. Erasure has a thermodynamic cost: at least kT log 2 per bit in the ideal limit. That doesn’t mean every operation has to cost that much, or that a thermodynamic computer automatically reaches that limit. But it tells you that computation is a physical process, and that if we want to push efficiency far enough, we have to design around the physics rather than treating it as an implementation detail.

r001.rationale: The response says thermal fluctuations become important as signal energy falls, but does not connect unavoidable noise to the discreteness of electric charge or explicitly discuss using very little charge.

r002.rationale: It presents thermal fluctuations as a reason to incorporate them into computation, but does not identify noise at very low charge as the reason computing must become thermodynamic.
